codex: The king of fruit in this land. Ripe is perfume and honey; unripe is sour enough for pickles. The sap in the skin can rash sensitive skin — peel it.
description: a tree heavy with smooth-skinned fruit blushing red and gold

knowledgeLevels.1: Mango. Sweet, fragrant, stains everything yellow. The king of fruit here.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe flesh (eat), unripe (sour — chutneys, pickles), the big flat stone (plant it). Peel the skin — the sap rashes some people.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~120 kcal a fruit, rich in vitamin A and C. Unripe mango with salt and water steadies you in the hot-season heat.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick at the blush stage and ripen in straw or rice husk. A grafted tree keeps its variety; a seedling is a lottery. The stone planted at the rains becomes a tree in ten years.

lookalikeNote: Unmistakable when ripe. At a distance the round orange fruit can suggest nux-vomica (nux_vomica) — check the leaves: mango has long lance-shaped alternate leaves and oblong fruit, never a perfect ball; nux-vomica has opposite oval leaves and flat coin seeds inside.
name: Mango
preparation: Eat ripe raw. Unripe: slice for chutney or pickle. Peel the skin — the sap irritates some people.

uses.note: ripe fruit raw; unripe for chutney/pickle
vitamin A and C; unripe + salt for heat

codex: The biggest tree-fruit on earth. Sweet bulbs inside when ripe; the seeds boil like chestnuts; unripe flesh cooks like meat. Oil your knife — the latex glues everything.
description: a tree carrying huge knobbly green pods, some bigger than your head

knowledgeLevels.1: Jackfruit. Enormous, knobbly, sweet inside. One fruit feeds a family.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe bulbs (eat), seeds (boil/roast — chestnut-like), unripe flesh (cooks like meat). Oil your knife and hands — the latex glues everything shut.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~150 kcal a chunk; the boiled seeds are a starchy staple. A single tree fruits for months.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: tap for a hollow thump and sniff the stem — ripe smells sweet. Dry the seeds; they store for months. Roast before grinding into flour.

lookalikeNote: Nothing else grows fruit this size on a trunk. Breadfruit is the smaller, rounder cousin — same rules apply.
name: Jackfruit
preparation: Ripe: pull the bulbs, eat. Seeds: boil or roast 30 min. Unripe: cook as a vegetable. Oil hands and blade against the latex.

uses.note: ripe bulbs raw; seeds boiled/roasted; unripe cooked

codex: The instant meal. The 'tree' is a giant herb that fruits once and dies — but its suckers are already rising. The flower and the stem core cook too.
description: a stand of huge soft leaves, hands of curved fruit hanging

knowledgeLevels.1: Banana. Peel and eat — the instant meal.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (ripe), flower (cook the blossom — strip the bitter heart first), stem core (chop and cook). The plant fruits once, then dies.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~105 kcal each, potassium, fast energy. The cooked blossom is iron-rich greens.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: cut the bunch when the top hands yellow; hang to ripen evenly. Transplant a sucker and one clump becomes ten in a year.

lookalikeNote: Unmistakable. Wild plantains are smaller and seedier — same rules, more chewing.
name: Banana
preparation: Peel and eat ripe. Flower: strip the bitter heart, chop and cook. Stem core: chop and boil.

uses.note: fruit raw; blossom and stem core cooked

codex: The traveler's canteen: sterile-ish water when young, rich meat when mature. Husk for fiber, shell for bowls and charcoal, oil that never spoils.
description: a tall leaning palm, green nuts clustered under the crown

knowledgeLevels.1: Coconut. Water inside, meat inside that. Never go thirsty near a palm.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: water (drink young), meat (eat; grate and press for milk), husk (fiber), shell (bowls, charcoal). Young = water; mature = meat.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~350 kcal of meat per nut; the water hydrates safely. Pressed oil keeps without spoiling and burns in lamps.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: shake for slosh (young) or heft for weight (mature). A bearing palm drops year-round — mark the good ones and climb with a rope loop, never bare.

lookalikeNote: Unmistakable. Fallen old nuts may be sprouted — the spongy 'apple' inside is edible too.
name: Coconut
preparation: Young (sloshes): drink the water, scoop the jelly. Mature (heavy, no slosh): crack for meat; grate and press for milk.

uses.note: water and meat; milk pressed from grated meat
young coconut water is safe to drink

codex: Rice gone feral in the drowned paddies. The staple of half the world, waiting in the mud — but the husk is silica glass. Husk it or it husks you.
description: a flooded flat of grass-like stalks hung with grain heads

knowledgeLevels.1: Rice, gone feral in the old paddies. The staple of half the world.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: grain only — pound and winnow off the husk first. The husk is inedible silica; eating unhusked paddy injures the gut.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~200 kcal a scoop cooked; the calorie backbone of every meal. Stores dry for a year.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest when heads droop and grains harden; sun-dry on mats before storing or it molds. One guarded paddy feeds many through the cool season.

lookalikeNote: Young rice looks like a dozen wild grasses — wait for the grain heads. No other grass here makes a fat white grain.
name: Feral Paddy Rice
preparation: Husk: pound and winnow until no husk remains. Boil. NEVER eat unhusked paddy — the husk tears the gut.

uses.note: husked and boiled; the staple grain

codex: Chana. Protein in a pod, from the cool-season fields. Soak overnight and boil soft — raw dried chickpeas are gravel and will not hurry.
description: a low bushy plant with small round pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Chickpea (chana). Protein in a pod.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: seeds — soak overnight, boil till soft. Raw dried chickpeas are hard as gravel and will not cook fast.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~180 kcal a handful cooked; protein and fiber that keeps you full. Roasted, they keep for weeks in a dry bag.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the leaves sweat a sour acid (malic) — the old hands collected it for thirst on hot marches. Harvest fully dry or the pods mold in the bag.

lookalikeNote: The pods are distinctive — small, inflated, one or two round seeds. Rosary pea (rosary_pea) is a VINE with scarlet-black beads, never a pod like this.
name: Chickpea
preparation: Soak overnight, boil until soft (an hour or more). Roast for a keeping snack.

uses.note: soaked and boiled; roasted for storage

codex: Masoor dal. The fastest-cooking protein in the land — twenty minutes, no soaking. The broth alone has fed the sick for centuries.
description: a low feathery plant with tiny flat pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Masoor dal — the red lentil. Cooks faster than anything else in the field.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: seeds — boil 20 minutes, no soaking. The skins slip when done; winnow out stones and chaff.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~170 kcal a handful; the fastest protein here. The broth feeds the sick when nothing else stays down.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: dry thoroughly before bagging — weevils are the enemy. A cool-season field of masoor is worth guarding like rice.

lookalikeNote: Do NOT confuse the pods with rosary pea (rosary_pea) — the pretty scarlet-black 'beans' are abrin poison, not lentils. No food bean is scarlet with a black eye.
name: Masoor Lentil
preparation: Boil 20 minutes until soft; no soaking needed. Skim and winnow out stones and chaff.

uses.note: boiled 20 min; the quick staple legume

codex: Sahjan. The leaves are a multivitamin you can pick off a tree. Pods cook like green beans; the root is horseradish-hot medicine, not food.
description: a fast thin tree with feathery leaves and long green pods hanging like drumsticks

knowledgeLevels.1: Drumstick tree (moringa/sahjan). The leaves are a multivitamin you can pick.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves (boil), pods (cook till soft, suck the pulp), flowers (fry). Roots are hot as horseradish — medicinal only, never food.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: leaves carry vitamin A, C, iron, calcium. A daily handful steadies a thin diet like nothing else green here.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: coppice it — cut back hard and it explodes with new leaves. Dry the leaves to a powder; it keeps a year and seasons every pot.

lookalikeNote: The feathery leaves and drumstick pods are distinctive. Don't confuse the root with horseradish-like food roots — moringa root is pungent medicine only.
name: Drumstick Tree
preparation: Leaves: boil 5 minutes. Pods: cook till soft, suck the pulp, discard the fiber. Roots are NOT food.
unit: a handful of leaves and pods

uses.note: leaves boiled; pods cooked
vitamin A/C, iron, calcium — the daily handful

codex: Haldi. The orange root that stains everything it touches — food, fingers, wounds. The old field dressing for cuts, and a pinch goes in every pot.
description: a clump of broad leaves; under it, orange fingers of root

knowledgeLevels.1: Turmeric (haldi). The orange root that stains everything it touches.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: rhizome — boil, dry, grind; or grate fresh into food. Fresh stains; dried keeps for months.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: antiseptic on wounds (the old field dressing), anti-inflammatory in food. A pinch in every pot.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: cure the rhizomes — boil 45 minutes, sun-dry a full week — or they rot in the bag. Powder with a little oil and black pepper; the body takes it up far better.

lookalikeNote: Ginger (ginger) grows beside it and looks similar — ginger is pale and hot-tasting; turmeric is orange and earthy-bitter. Both are safe; confusing them only ruins the recipe.
name: Turmeric
preparation: Boil the rhizome, sun-dry, grind — or grate fresh into food. Fresh stains skin and cloth.

uses.note: spice; fresh grated or dried powder
antiseptic wound dusting; anti-inflammatory

codex: Imli. Sour enough to wake the dead — and the sour is the point: it preserves food and steadies the gut. Pressed pulp blocks keep a year.
description: a wide shady tree with curved brown pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Tamarind (imli). Sour enough to wake the dead — and to keep food from spoiling.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (soak, strain out seeds and fiber), seeds (roast and grind in famine). The sour is the preservative.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: vitamin C; keeps chutneys and cooked fish safe a day longer. Hot tamarind water is the thirst-quencher of the hot season.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: press the pulp into blocks with a little salt — it stores a year. Seed powder stretches flour when grain runs thin.

lookalikeNote: Unmistakable — no other tree here makes curved brown pods of sour pulp. The shade it throws is itself a landmark.
name: Tamarind
preparation: Soak the pulp, strain out seeds and fiber. Seeds: roast and grind only in real hunger.

uses.note: pulp soaked/strained; souring and preserving
vitamin C; digestive

codex: The monsoon berry. Sweet-tart, purple to the elbow. Ripe is deep purple and soft; red is a day early. Ferments by noon — eat or dry fast.
description: a big tree dropping purple-black berries that stain your tongue

knowledgeLevels.1: Jamun. The monsoon berry — sweet-tart, purple to the elbow.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (eat ripe — deep purple, not red), seed (dry and powder — the old blood-sugar remedy). Eat the fruit, spit the seed.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~60 kcal a handful; iron and vitamin C. The seed powder is medicine, not food.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: shake the branches onto a cloth at dawn — the ripe ones fall on their own. They ferment by noon; eat fresh or sun-dry.

lookalikeNote: Ripe jamun is deep purple-black and soft, on a TREE. Lantana (lantana) berries cluster at the same season in mixed red-orange-purple — smaller, harder, on a rough-leafed SHRUB with square stems. Tree vs shrub is the test.
name: Jamun
preparation: Eat ripe and soft; spit the seed. Dry surplus in the sun — they keep weeks.

uses.note: ripe fruit raw; dried for storage
iron, vitamin C; seed powder is the folk blood-sugar remedy

codex: Bel. The hard-shelled fruit you crack like a coconut. Ripe pulp eats like custard; unripe dried and powdered is the classic dysentery cure of this land.
description: a thorny tree with hard round green-grey fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Bael (bel). The hard-shelled fruit — crack it like a coconut.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe pulp (eat; aromatic, yields to the thumb), unripe (sun-dry, powder — the dysentery cure), leaves (bitter tea). Strain out the gummy seeds.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~90 kcal a half-fruit; the unripe powder stops dysentery — a life-saver where the water is dirty.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the shell keeps it fresh for weeks on the tree — a living pantry. Thorns mean harvest with a hooked stick, not bare hands.

lookalikeNote: Nux-vomica (nux_vomica) hangs round hard ORANGE fruit at the same season — its seeds are flat grey coins of strychnine. Bael is green-grey and larger; cracked open, bael seeds are small and woolly, never flat coins. When in doubt, don't.
name: Bael
preparation: Crack the shell, scoop the pulp, strain out gummy seeds. Unripe: slice, sun-dry, powder for dysentery.

uses.note: ripe pulp raw
unripe powder for dysentery

codex: Amrud. Vitamin C by the handful — more than an orange. The leaf tea steadies the gut. Pick at the first yellow blush; the fruit flies find them a day later.
description: a smooth-barked small tree with round green-yellow fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Guava (amrud). Vitamin C by the handful.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (eat whole, seeds and all — the seeds are the fiber), leaves (boil for a dysentery tea).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~70 kcal each; the leaf tea steadies the gut when water is suspect.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick at the first yellow blush — fruit flies arrive a day later. Fallen fruit ferments fast; gather twice a day in season.

lookalikeNote: No poisonous twin. Unripe guavas are hard and astringent — wait for the blush and the perfume.
name: Guava
preparation: Eat ripe whole, seeds and all. Leaves: boil 10 minutes for tea.

uses.note: ripe fruit whole
vitamin C; leaf tea for the gut

codex: Amla. Sour enough to make your eyes water — and one of the richest vitamin C sources on earth. It keeps its C even dried, which is why the old hands prize it.
description: a tree with feathery leaflets and pale green round fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Amla. Eye-wateringly sour — and one of the richest vitamin C sources on earth.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (eat fresh if brave; better dried, pickled, or boiled with jaggery). The sour IS the medicine.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: preserves vitamin C even dried — the old scurvy cure of this land. A winter handful keeps gums and wounds sound.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest before the fruit drops; shade-dry to keep the C. One tree's harvest, dried, lasts the year.

lookalikeNote: No twin — the feathery leaflets plus pale ribbed fruit are distinctive. If it isn't mouth-puckering, it isn't ripe amla.
name: Amla
preparation: Eat fresh, dry, pickle, or boil with jaggery. Shade-dry surplus for the year.

uses.note: fresh, dried, or pickled — the sour staple
vitamin C that survives drying

codex: The fast fruit — seed to eating in a single year. Ripe is gentle food for the sick; green is a vegetable with a warning: the milky sap burns.
description: a soft-trunked small tree with huge lobed leaves and melon-like fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Papaya. The fast fruit — seed to eating in a year.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe fruit (eat — yellow-orange, gives to the thumb), unripe (cook like squash — NEVER raw; the latex burns mouths and is unsafe in pregnancy), seeds (peppery; a spoonful is the old worm remedy).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~120 kcal each; ripe is gentle on sick stomachs. The leaf tea is the folk fever remedy of the wet season.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: score green fruit to bleed the latex out before cooking. One tree fruits for years — put a guard on it in season.

lookalikeNote: No poisonous twin — but the rule is the ID: if it bleeds white milk, cook it; if it's sunset-colored and soft, eat it.
name: Papaya
preparation: Ripe (soft, yellow-orange): eat raw. Unripe (green, milky): bleed the sap, then cook thoroughly. Never eat green papaya raw.

uses.note: ripe raw; unripe only cooked
gentle food for the sick; seeds as worm remedy

codex: The flowers fall like rain at dawn and taste like brown sugar — then they ferment. Dry them fast and they're storable sugar; the seeds press into lamp oil.
description: a big shady tree; at dawn the ground beneath is strewn with fleshy cream flowers

knowledgeLevels.1: Mahua. The flowers fall like rain and taste like brown sugar — then they ferment.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: flowers (dry in sun, then cook — raw heaps ferment within a day), seeds (press for oil — cooking and lamp oil), ripe fruit pulp (eat sparingly).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: dried flowers are storable sugar (~120 kcal a handful); the seed oil burns clean in lamps.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: gather at dawn before the bees and the boars. Dry on clean mats — moldy mahua is a stomach bomb. A good tree is worth a dawn patrol.

lookalikeNote: No twin — the dawn carpet of cream flowers under a big tree is unmistakable. If the flowers smell of liquor already, they're fermenting: dry or abandon.
name: Mahua
preparation: Sun-dry the fallen flowers the same day, then cook. Seeds: press for oil. Never eat moldy dried flowers.

uses.note: dried flowers cooked; the storable sugar
seed oil burns clean in lamps

codex: Kamal. The pond is a pantry: crisp starchy roots below, seeds above. Feel for the root with your feet — don't dive blind into old tanks.
description: a still pond sheeted with round leaves and pink flowers; below, the roots

knowledgeLevels.1: Lotus (kamal). The pond is a pantry — roots below, seeds above.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: rhizome (peel, slice, boil or fry — crisp and starchy), seeds (crack, boil; pick out the bitter green sprout), young leaves (wrap food, not food).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~80 kcal a root; steady starch where rice fails. The seeds store dry for months.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: feel for the root in the mud with your feet — never dive blind in old tanks. Always leave a growing node; the pond feeds you again.

lookalikeNote: Water-lily pads look similar but lotus leaves stand ABOVE the water on stalks and the flowers are big and pink. Only lotus makes the fat edible root.
name: Lotus
preparation: Peel, slice, boil or fry the rhizome. Seeds: crack, remove the bitter green heart, boil.

uses.note: rhizome cooked; seeds boiled

codex: Pond popcorn. The black seeds pop white in a hot pan — the Bihar staple. The pads are armor: harvest with a hooked pole, never bare hands.
description: a pond of huge spiny pads; under them, spiny pods of black seeds

knowledgeLevels.1: Makhana (fox nut). Pond popcorn — the black seeds pop white in a hot pan.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: seeds only (roast/pop; raw they're hard shot). The pads are armor — harvest with a hooked pole, never bare hands.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~100 kcal a handful popped; light, and it keeps for months dry.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: grade by size — the big ones pop, the small ones grind into flour. A harvested pond re-seeds itself if you leave the small pods.

lookalikeNote: Don't confuse the pods with lotus pods — makhana pads are viciously spiny, lotus pads are smooth. The seeds are black marbles; nothing else here makes those.
name: Makhana (Fox Nut)
preparation: Crack the spiny pods, pop the seeds in a hot dry pan like popcorn. Raw seeds are inedible shot.

uses.note: seeds popped/roasted; the keeping pond grain

codex: Singhara. The pond's horned nut — sweet and crisp. Boil it always: raw nuts from still water carry liver flukes.
description: floating rosettes of leaves; under them, black horned nuts

knowledgeLevels.1: Singhara (water chestnut). The pond's horned nut — sweet and crisp.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: kernel only (boil 20 minutes, crack the horned shell). NEVER eat raw from still water — liver flukes.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~90 kcal a handful; the fasting food of the cool season, gentle and filling.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: rake the rosettes with a pole — the ripe nuts drop. Dry in shell for months; the horns protect the kernel.

lookalikeNote: The horned black shell is unmistakable. Trapa's horns are the ID — nothing edible or poisonous here copies them.
name: Water Chestnut
preparation: Boil 20 minutes, crack the horned shell, eat the kernel. Always cooked — never raw from still water.

uses.note: kernel boiled and cracked

codex: Crisp and sweet — after you boil the poison out. Raw shoots carry cyanide; slice thin, boil TWICE, discard the water. No shortcuts.
description: a clump of giant grass; after rain, pale spears push up

knowledgeLevels.1: Bamboo shoots. Crisp and sweet — after you boil the poison out.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young shoots only (peel to the tender core, slice thin, boil TWICE and discard the water — cyanogenic glycosides). Old shoots are wood.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~40 kcal a shoot; bulk and crunch in the hungry wet season.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest at knee height — taller is bitter wood. Ferment the surplus in brine; it keeps a year and the sour is gold in the cool season.

lookalikeNote: No twin — but the rule is absolute: any shoot eaten raw or single-boiled can poison. If you can't boil twice with fresh water, don't pick.
name: Bamboo Shoot
preparation: Peel to the tender core, slice thin, boil, DISCARD the water, boil again. Then cook as food. Raw is poison.

uses.note: double-boiled, then cooked

codex: Arbi. The corm is potato-like once you cook the sting out — raw, the needle crystals set your mouth on fire. Cook with something sour; acid tames the itch.
description: big heart-shaped leaves on stalks, like elephant ears

knowledgeLevels.1: Arbi (colocasia/taro). The corm is potato-like — once you cook the sting out.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: corms (boil whole, peel AFTER cooking), leaves (boil with something sour — the sour tames the itch). Raw = mouth on fire (oxalate needles).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~110 kcal a handful; the wet-season starch that grows where rice drowns.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: cook with tamarind — acid dissolves the oxalate itch. Replant the tops; each corm becomes a clump.

lookalikeNote: Elephant-ear leaves are the ID. Wild aroids with similar leaves are ALL irritant raw — the rule 'boil whole, peel after, eat with sour' covers the whole family safely.
name: Colocasia (Arbi)
preparation: Boil or roast WHOLE until soft, peel after cooking. Leaves: boil with tamarind or another sour. Never eat raw.

uses.note: corms boiled whole; leaves boiled with sour

codex: Chaulai. The weed that feeds — greens now, grain later. Strip the tops and it bushes out; let one plant seed and next rains you have a field.
description: a knee-high weed with soft green leaves and a seedy spike

knowledgeLevels.1: Chaulai (wild amaranth). The weed that feeds — greens now, grain later.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves (cook 5 minutes), seeds (rub the dry spikes, winnow, pop or grind — a handful of seed is a meal's worth).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: iron and vitamin A in the greens; the seeds are ~15% protein — real grain from a weed.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: cut-and-come-again — strip the tops and it bushes out thicker. Let one plant go to seed for next rains.

lookalikeNote: Young plants resemble lambs quarters (lambs_quarters) — both are safe, so the confusion costs nothing.
name: Wild Amaranth
preparation: Leaves: boil or sauté 5 minutes. Seeds: rub dry spikes, winnow, pop like tiny grain or grind.

uses.note: leaves cooked; seeds popped/ground

codex: Kadi patta. Not food by the handful — the flavor that makes food food. Tempered in hot oil, the crackle means it's working.
description: a shrub with glossy leaflets that smell of curry when crushed

knowledgeLevels.1: Curry leaf (kadi patta). The flavor that makes food food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves (temper in hot oil — the crackle means it's working; or boil in water). Strip the bitter stems.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: iron and the appetite back — a handful in the pot stretches thin rations. The old stomach tonic.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: shade-dries well; the powder keeps a year. Plant the berries — the birds plant them everywhere anyway.

lookalikeNote: Crush a leaf: curry leaf smells of curry, unmistakable. Neem leaves are bitter and larger — don't confuse the trees, though both are useful.
name: Curry Leaf
preparation: Fry in hot oil or boil in water. Chew a few raw for the stomach. Strip bitter stems.

uses.note: tempered in oil; the flavor base
iron; stomach tonic

codex: Tea and mosquito armor in one clump. Bruise the stalks and boil; rub crushed leaves on skin and the mosquitoes genuinely hesitate — for an hour.
description: a fountain of sharp-edged grass smelling of lemon

knowledgeLevels.1: Lemongrass. Tea and mosquito armor in one clump.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: stalks (bruise and boil), leaves (steep). The edges cut — harvest with a twist, never a bare grab.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the tea settles stomachs; the citronella oil genuinely repels mosquitoes for about an hour.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: split the clump to propagate — it divides like grass because it is grass. A ring around camp is worth more than a wall of it in the pot.

lookalikeNote: Lemon smell is the ID — crush and sniff. Scentless sharp grasses are just grass.
name: Lemongrass
preparation: Bruise stalks, boil 10 minutes for tea. Crushed leaves rubbed on skin repel mosquitoes.

uses.note: bruised stalks boiled
mosquito repellent; stomach-settling tea

codex: The courtyard herb. Tea for coughs, courage for fevers — and sacred to many households. Take only what you need, and say thanks.
description: a small bushy herb with purple-tinged leaves, smelling of cloves

knowledgeLevels.1: Tulsi (holy basil). The courtyard herb — tea for coughs.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves (steep or chew), seeds (soak — they swell like frogspawn; the old cooling drink).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the household remedy for cough, cold, and low spirits. The smoke dislikes mosquitoes as much as you do.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pinch the flower heads and it bushes forever. It is sacred to many — harvest gently, never strip a courtyard plant bare.

lookalikeNote: Clove scent is the ID. Other basils are safe too — the confusion costs nothing.
name: Tulsi (Holy Basil)
preparation: Steep fresh or dried leaves in hot water. Chew a few for coughs. Seeds soaked make the cooling drink.

uses.note: steeped for coughs and fevers
household remedy; mosquito-disliking smoke

codex: Adrak. Heat without fire — for food and for guts. A thumb in the pot, a slice in the tea: the traveler's stomach insurance.
description: reed-like leaves; underground, knobby pale rhizomes

knowledgeLevels.1: Ginger (adrak). Heat without fire — for food and for guts.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: rhizome (fresh or dried). A thumb in the pot, a slice in the tea.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: settles nausea, warms the cold-season body. The first thing to reach for when the stomach turns.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: store in dry sand — it keeps for months. Replant a knob with an eye and it multiplies.

lookalikeNote: Turmeric (turmeric) grows beside it — ginger is pale and hot, turmeric orange and earthy. Both safe; confusing them only ruins the recipe.
name: Ginger
preparation: Grate fresh into food or boil for tea. Slice, sun-dry, and powder for the year.

uses.note: spice; fresh or dried
nausea; warming

codex: Bargad. A single tree that's a forest — and it fruits. Eat only the soft red ripe figs, and check for wasps first: a fig without wasps didn't ripen right.
description: the giant tree with roots dropping from its branches like curtains

knowledgeLevels.1: Banyan (bargad). A single tree that's a forest — and it fruits.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe figs only (soft, red — check for wasps first), aerial roots (fiber), bark (the old dysentery tea). Unripe figs are astringent and full of wasps.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~40 kcal a handful in fruit season; the deep shade is the real gift in the hot months.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: sacred to many — harvest gently, take fallen fruit first. A fruiting banyan feeds every bird for a mile; watch what they eat.

lookalikeNote: Peepal (peepal_fig) fruits similarly — both are Ficus, both follow the same rules: ripe and soft only. The trees differ (banyan's curtain roots), the caution is identical.
name: Banyan Fig
preparation: Eat only fully ripe (soft, red) figs. Check for wasps. Unripe figs are astringent — leave them.

uses.note: ripe figs only

codex: The tree the Buddha sat under. Its figs feed the birds, and you in a pinch — ripe and soft only, and take fallen fruit first out of respect.
description: a tall tree with heart-shaped leaves that shiver in any breeze

knowledgeLevels.1: Peepal. The tree the Buddha sat under — its figs feed birds, and you in a pinch.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe figs (soft, dark — fallen fruit first), leaves (the shivering hearts are the ID), bark (bitter tea, medicine not food).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~35 kcal a handful; a hunger-gap fruit more than a staple.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: sacred to many — never cut, never strip. The figs come in waves; the birds will show you when.

lookalikeNote: Banyan (banyan_fig) is the cousin — same Ficus rules: ripe and soft only. Peepal's heart-shaped shivering leaves are the ID.
name: Peepal Fig
preparation: Eat only fully ripe fallen figs. Unripe figs are astringent.

uses.note: ripe fallen figs

codex: The village pharmacy — bitter enough to cure. Twigs are the original toothbrush; leaves keep weevils out of grain and treat skin. Never drink the seed oil.
description: a spreading tree with bitter leaves; the air under it smells clean

knowledgeLevels.1: Neem. The village pharmacy — bitter enough to cure.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: twigs (chew one end to a brush — the original toothbrush), leaves (boil for skin washes; the bitter tea is medicine, not food), seeds (oil is EXTERNAL only — never drink).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: keeps stored grain weevil-free for months; the leaf wash treats skin infections and itches.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: shade-dry leaves to powder; it keeps a year. A neem by the house is planted on purpose — the shade is medicine too.

lookalikeNote: No edible twin — the bitterness is the ID. If the leaf isn't bitter, it isn't neem.
name: Neem
preparation: Twigs: chew to a brush. Leaves: boil for washes; bitter tea as medicine, not food. Seed oil: external only.

uses.note: toothbrush twigs; skin wash; grain protectant

codex: Taad. The pillar palm: jelly fruit in summer, sweet sap at dawn with a two-hour fuse — drink fresh or let it become toddy.
description: a towering fan palm, black and straight as a pillar

knowledgeLevels.1: Palmyra (taad). The pillar palm — jelly fruit in summer, sweet sap at dawn.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit pulp (eat fresh — the jelly spoils by evening), sap/neera (drink within hours; it ferments to toddy fast), sprout (the tuber-like shoot, roast).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~80 kcal a fruit; the sap is sugar water with a two-hour fuse. The jaggery made from it keeps a year.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: tap at dawn, drink by noon. Eat the jelly in the field — it doesn't travel. The sprouts are the hidden harvest.

lookalikeNote: No twin — the black pillar trunk with a fan crown is unmistakable. Fallen fruit ferments fast; if it smells of liquor, abandon it.
name: Palmyra Palm
preparation: Eat the jelly pulp fresh the same day. Sap: drink within hours. Sprouts: roast.

uses.note: jelly pulp fresh; sap drunk within hours

codex: Putush. Pretty flowers, pretty berries — and the green ones can wreck your liver. The invader: where lantana thickets stand, the forest lost.
description: a scrambling shrub with rough leaves and clusters of tiny flowers in mixed colors

knowledgeLevels.1: Lantana (putush/ghaneri). Pretty flowers, pretty berries — and the green ones can wreck your liver.
knowledgeLevels.2: ID: square stems, rough sandpapery leaves that stink when crushed, flower heads mixing yellow-orange-pink. Berries green, then purple-black.
knowledgeLevels.3: Danger: unripe berries and leaves carry lantadenes — liver failure in livestock, misery in people. The ripe purple ones are less bad but NEVER safe.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: it's the invader — where lantana thickets stand, the forest lost. Clear it for firewood; never for food. Goats that learn it, learn the hard way.

lookalikeNote: The berry clusters mimic jamun (jamun) at a hungry glance — but jamun is a TREE with single round purple fruit; lantana is a SHRUB with clustered mixed-color berries and rough stinking leaves. Tree vs shrub is the test.
name: Lantana
preparation: DO NOT EAT any part. If eaten: it was probably the berries — expect vomiting; watch the liver.
sources: Native Plant Society of Texas invasive profile

codex: Kuchila. The fruit looks friendly; the seeds are strychnine. Monkeys eat the pulp and spit the seeds — you are not a monkey. Learn this tree like a loaded gun.
description: a medium tree with glossy oval leaves and round orange fruit like small apples

knowledgeLevels.1: Poison-nut tree (kuchila). The fruit looks friendly. The seeds are strychnine.
knowledgeLevels.2: ID: opposite glossy oval leaves, foul-smelling greenish flowers, round hard orange fruit with jelly pulp and flat grey coin-seeds.
knowledgeLevels.3: Danger: seeds are ~1.5% strychnine — convulsions, and no antidote. Even the bark is poison. The pulp is eaten by monkeys and hornbills; the seeds pass through them whole.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: learn this tree the way you learn a loaded gun — by sight, at distance. Mark every one near camp and teach it to every newcomer.

lookalikeNote: Bael (bael) hangs hard round fruit at the same season — but bael is GREEN-GREY and larger, with small woolly seeds; nux-vomica is ORANGE with flat grey coin-seeds of strychnine. When in doubt, don't touch.
name: Strychnine Tree
preparation: DO NOT EAT any part. No safe preparation exists. Mark the tree; teach it.

codex: The trumpet-flower bush. Every part is a delirium poison — blindness, madness, death. No safe dose, no home antidote. It loves disturbed ground near ruins: exactly where you forage.
description: a bushy plant with big trumpet flowers, white or purple, and spiny round pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Datura. The trumpet-flower bush — every part is a delirium poison.
knowledgeLevels.2: ID: big trumpet blooms, spiny apple-like pods full of flat brown seeds. Smells rank when crushed.
knowledgeLevels.3: Danger: tropane alkaloids — dilated pupils, delirium, death. No safe dose and no home antidote. A single pod's seeds can kill.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: it loves disturbed ground near ruins — exactly where you forage. Learn the trumpet at fifty paces; never touch the pods.

lookalikeNote: No edible twin in this land — that's the lesson. The pods tempt seed-collectors; the seeds inside are flat and brown, nothing like any food seed here.
name: Datura
preparation: DO NOT EAT any part. No safe preparation exists.

codex: Ratti. The prettiest poison here — beads red as blood with a black eye, once used to weigh gold. One chewed seed can kill an adult. No food bean is scarlet with a black eye.
description: a twining vine with feathery leaves and pods that split to show scarlet-black beads

knowledgeLevels.1: Rosary pea (ratti/gunja). The prettiest poison here — beads red as blood with a black eye.
knowledgeLevels.2: ID: twining vine, feathery leaflets, pods curling back to show hard shiny scarlet seeds with a black spot. Once used as the ratti gold-weight.
knowledgeLevels.3: Danger: abrin — one chewed seed can kill an adult, and there is no antidote. Intact seeds may pass through, but never gamble it.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: children string them into beads; don't. If you see the beads, you're looking at a legume — and legumes are food here, which is exactly why this one kills the careless.

lookalikeNote: The seeds mimic small beans and lentils (masoor_lentil, chickpea) to a hungry eye — but no food bean is scarlet with a black eye. Color is the warning.
name: Rosary Pea
preparation: DO NOT EAT any part. No safe preparation exists. Do not string the seeds.
